text: Adsorption experiments were performed in batch mode at 25 C. A fixed mass of 50 mg of adsorbent was added to 100 mL of solution. The flasks were shaken at 150 rpm for 24 h unless stated otherwise.
The initial concentration were varied between 10 and 200 mg/L. Aliquots was withdrawn at fixed intervals and filtered through a 0.45 um membrane.

Residual concentrations were determined by UV-vis spectrophotometry at 464 nm. Calibration curves were linear over the whole working range. Each measurement was repeated three times and the mean is reported.

It is worth noting that the fact that equilibrium was reached within 4 h is consistent with a surface-controlled process. Due to the fact that the external film resistance is small, stirring speed had little influence.
Kinetic data were analysed with pseudo-first-order and pseudo-second-order models. The pseudo-second-order model described the data better in all cases. Rate constants are listed in Table 3.
The uptake increase rapidly during the first 30 min. After this period the curves was essentially flat.
Intraparticle diffusion plots were not linear through the origin. This indicates that diffusion is not the only rate-limiting step. A boundary-layer contribution therefore cannot be excluded.
Thermodynamic parameters was calculated from the temperature dependence of the distribution coefficient. The negative Gibbs energy indicate a spontaneous process at all temperatures studied.
The enthalpy change was positive, which suggests an endothermic interaction. Entropy increased upon adsorption, consistent with the release of ordered water molecules from the surface.
Regeneration was tested with 0.1 mol/L sodium hydroxide. The recovered material retained 92% of its initial capacity after five cycles. No structural collapse was detected by nitrogen adsorption.
In addition, and furthermore, the leaching of silicon was below the detection limit. The supernatant were analysed by ICP-OES after each cycle.
Competing ions were introduced to assess selectivity. Sulfate and chloride had a minor effect at equimolar concentrations. Phosphate reduced the uptake by roughly one third.
The selectivity may be explained by the specific interaction between the amine groups and the target anion. This interpretation is supported by the shift observed in the FTIR spectra.
A comparison with materials reported previously are given in Table 4. The present adsorbent shows a capacity that are competitive with mesoporous analogues [28].
Column experiments were carried out at a flow rate of 2 mL/min. Breakthrough occurred after approximately 180 bed volumes. The Thomas model reproduced the breakthrough curve adequately.
The bed depth service time model was applied to the column data. Extrapolation to larger columns should be treated with caution, because axial dispersion was not measured in this work.

Taking into consideration the fact that the material can be regenerated, the process appears economically plausible. It should be pointed out that a full cost analysis was outside the scope of the present study.
